bib.title: Coding Agents with Multimodal Browsing are Generalist Problem Solvers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Coding Agents with Multimodal Browsing are Generalist Problem Solvers" (OpenHands-Versa). Aditya Bharat Soni, Boxuan Li, Xingyao Wang, Valerie Chen, Graham Neubig. CMU, an independent author, and All Hands AI. arXiv 2506.03011v1, 3 Jun 2025. Preprint ("Under review").

COVERAGE: All 15 of 15 pages, 54,379 chars. Read in full, including appendices A-F and the reference list. The extraction was clean. Figures 1-3 are images, so only their captions were read.

RECOMMENDED HOME: Weak fit for 03-tool-design. It is a loose fit for 08 maturity, or for 07 orchestration as a single-agent versus multi-agent datapoint. The strongest harness lesson is that adding general tools beat specialist multi-agent systems. A secondary lesson is that one tool's output quality (search snippets) moves results a lot. Neither is a tool-contract, ACI-design or write-safety finding. The paper has no tool schemas, error messages, edit-tool ablation or safety analysis. If cited in 03, use it only for capability granularity (a few general tools) and output discipline (the browsing condenser and the search API choice). The agent was built on the OpenHands tool set, with edit_file/view_file and bash left unchanged.

CORE CLAIM: A single agent with a small set of general tools matches or beats specialist agents across three benchmarks. The tools are code edit and execution, API web search, Set-of-Marks multimodal browsing, and multimodal file viewing. The authors argue specialist agents fail to generalise because their tools are over-tailored to one benchmark.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (Table 2, test splits)
Setup for all: pass@1, temperature 0, one run per cell. Max steps were 100 for SWE-Bench M and The Agent Company (TAC), and 60 for GAIA. OpenHands v0.28.1 was the base. No variance, seeds or confidence intervals are reported.
- OpenHands-Versa with claude-sonnet-4: GAIA 51.16%, SWE-Bench M 34.43%, TAC full 33.14% and partial 43.19%.
- OpenHands-Versa with claude-3.7-sonnet: GAIA 51.16%, SWE-Bench M 31.33%, TAC full 30.86% and partial 40.18%.
- OpenHands v0.28.1 (claude-3.7-sonnet), same model as the Versa row above: GAIA 37.21%, SWE-Bench M 31.72%, TAC full 26.29% and partial 36.41%.
- Versa versus OpenHands, same model: GAIA +13.9 points, TAC full +4.6, TAC partial +3.8. SWE-Bench M is 0.39 points lower, which the authors call retained coding ability.
- Versa versus best published baselines, as the abstract frames it: SWE-Bench M +9.1 over Agentless-Lite (25.34%), GAIA +1.3 over OpenDeepResearch (49.83%), TAC +9.1 (abstract wording). The body text says TAC +6.9 full and +6.8 partial, which does not match the abstract's 9.1.
- OWL-roleplaying (multi-agent, gpt-4o and o3-mini) scores 4.00% full and 11.04% partial on TAC. The authors cite this as failure to generalise. It is a different model, so it is not a controlled comparison.
- GAIA validation (Appendix C, claude-3.7-sonnet): Versa 64.24%, versus OWL 58.18%, OpenDeepResearch 55.15% and Magentic-One 46.06%.
- Cost: not reported in dollars. Runtime was about 24 h for GAIA, about 54 h for TAC and about 12 h for SWE-Bench M, on CPU-only AWS t3.2xlarge machines.

ABLATIONS
The only ablation is the search API, on the GAIA validation split with Versa.
- Brave 56.96%, Exa 58.18%, Tavily 64.24%. Switching from Brave to Tavily gives +7.28 points.
- Brave snippets come from raw page text. Exa and Tavily give LLM-generated summaries, and Tavily adds an LLM-generated answer per query.
- The authors say this is "one of the primary reasons". It is a mechanism claim and was not isolated.
- There is no ablation of the individual added tools (browser, file viewer, search, planning prompt, condenser). The 13.9-point GAIA gain is therefore not attributed to any one component.

DESIGN DETAILS
- The browsing condenser keeps only the k=1 most recent browser observation. Older ones become a placeholder. Its purpose is to cut cost and context size.
- A fixed planning prompt is appended every τ=10 steps.
- The tools include a search API because the agent was often blocked by CAPTCHAs when using search engines in the browser.
- File viewing converts files to Markdown, in the style of Magentic-One's FileSurfer.
- GAIA answers are extracted by a separate claude-3.7-sonnet call.

TOOL-USE ANALYSIS (Fig. 2, descriptive only)
- Without a search tool, OpenHands relies on the browser and "frequently navigates to hallucinated or invalid URLs".
- About 40% of Versa's GAIA tool calls go to search.

QUOTES
- "outperforming the best-performing previously published results with absolute improvements in success rate of 9.1, 1.3, and 9.1 points respectively." (p.1, abstract)
- "generalist agents can be designed simply by providing the necessary tools to the agent and leaving it for the backbone LLM to autonomously decide how to use these tools to solve the task." (p.9, conclusion)
- "Although seemingly unimportant, the choice of search API significantly impacts downstream performance." (p.9, §5.3)
- "OpenHands relies more heavily on the browser in the absence of a search engine, due to which it frequently navigates to hallucinated or invalid URLs." (p.8, §5.1)

LIMITS AND NOT SHOWN
- Authors concede: no GUI/desktop tasks such as OSWorld, and limited video handling.
- Authors concede: it relies mostly on closed models, and open models do poorly.
- Authors concede: not every baseline was run on every benchmark, because of cost.
- Only the Claude family was used for Versa, so model generality is not shown.
- Comparisons to published baselines mix different models and agent versions, so they are not controlled. Only the OpenHands-versus-Versa comparison holds the model fixed.
- Single runs, no variance, and no per-tool ablation.
- GAIA leaderboard entries with up to 77% were excluded because they lack code.
- Error analysis was manual and qualitative. Failures: relying on wrong search snippets, CAPTCHAs, not writing or running tests, stuck loops in OwnCloud, and premature exit.
- It does not show tool-description or schema design effects, edit-tool format comparisons, MCP, skills, or write safety.
- It does not test multi-agent versus single-agent in a controlled way. The claim that multi-agent systems fail to generalise rests on missing tools (no shell, no file editing, no non-Python execution), which confounds architecture with tool coverage.

BUILDS ON
- OpenHands (Wang et al., ICLR 2024/2025; v0.28.1) as the base framework.
- BrowserGym (de Chezelles et al., TMLR 2025) for the browser action space.
- Set-of-Mark prompting (Yang et al., 2023).
- Magentic-One FileSurfer's Markdown conversion (Fourney et al., arXiv 2024).
- SWE-agent's agent-computer interfaces (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2024) as a baseline.
- The Think tool (Anthropic, 2025) is mentioned as an alternative to the planning prompt.
- Benchmarks: GAIA (Mialon et al.), SWE-Bench Multimodal (Yang et al., ICLR 2025) and TheAgentCompany (Xu et al. 2024).

CODE: none in the paper. Open-source repo: github.com/adityasoni9998/OpenHands-Versa.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig. 2 (p.8), tool-use distribution of OpenHands versus OpenHands-Versa on each benchmark. It shows that a generalist toolset is used differently per domain. Its extent is not verified, because only the caption text was read. Fig. 1 (p.2) is the bar-chart summary but adds nothing beyond Table 2.

PROBLEMS: None. No embedded instructions. Table 1 icons extracted as garbled FontAwesome names (/code, /times-circle), but the table's meaning is clear from the text. The abstract and body disagree on the TAC gain (9.1 versus 6.9 and 6.8 points); cite the body's Table 2 numbers.
